rows.why: S1's distinctive rows (2d = 172800000, 1d… = 86400000) settle whether days are a supported unit and what a day is worth. The pick adds d at 86400000 ms. The zero-count rows (0s, 1d0h0m0s0ms) also touch item 8, but the main question here is which units exist.
S2 settles whether whitespace around the duration is allowed. The pick trims it before parsing, so "  45m\n" gives 2700000.

S3 is a catch-all, and items 1, 3, 5 and 7 each settle some of its rows; all of them agree. Item 8 is the one whose answer decides the 05s row, and S3 expects leading zeros to be rejected. The pick accepts `01h`, so `05s` would parse instead of erroring.
No item asks whether a count may go over the size of the next unit up (90m allowed instead of needing 1h30m). Item 6 covers order and repeats, not count size.
S5 settles unit order and repeats. The pick requires strictly descending units, so 30m1h, 1h1h, 1s500ms2s and 5ms1s are all errors.
S6 settles the maximum value. The pick caps it at 2^53-1 ms, so exactly 9007199254740991 parses.
S7 settles what happens above the maximum. The pick returns 0 with an error past 2^53-1 and checks for overflow at each digit and on each sum, which covers both rows.
S8 settles how milliseconds are printed. The pick breaks the value into d/h/m/s/ms, leaves out zero parts and prints 0 as `0ms`, which matches every row.
S9 settles how large values are printed. The pick makes days the largest unit, so 2^53-1 comes out as 104249991d8h59m991ms.
No item asks whether formatted output must parse back to the same number. Items 11 and 12 cover formatting only.

S11 settles formatting of negative or too-large values. The pick returns an empty string and an error below 0 or above 2^53-1. The scenario's wording rule that the message contains "milliseconds" isn't covered by the pick, but the behaviour matches.
